feedback.problem: Given that $f(x)={x}^{3}+\frac{3}{x}$ is defined for $x\in (0,\infty ),$ find the values of $x$ for which the function is strictly increasing.
feedback.worked_solution:
The function is strictly increasing where ${f}^{′}(x)>0.$ Differentiating $f(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =3{x}^{2}-\frac{3}{{x}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

so we need to solve the inequality

$$
3{x}^{2}-\frac{3}{{x}^{2}}>0.
$$

Using that $x>0,$ the above inequality factors as

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-\frac{3}{{x}^{2}} & >0 \\ {x}^{2}-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} & >0 \\ {x}^{2}({x}^{2}-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}) & >0 \\ {x}^{4}-1 & >0 \\ ({x}^{2}+1)(x+1)(x-1) & >0.\end{aligned}
$$

The factors ${x}^{2}+1$ and $x+1$ are positive, so this reduces to

$$
x-1>0.
$$

Solving this inequality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x-1 & >0 \\ x & >1.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that $f(x)$ is strictly increasing on $(1,\infty ).$
